summary: For ages 9-10, 'using structure' means deliberately choosing an efficient route or form by exploiting relationships rather than grinding: rewriting 25×16 as 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400 via factor pairs; treating 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as one quantity and picking whichever form makes a task a one-step job; and deducing missing angles from facts (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, around a point 360°, vertically opposite angles equal) instead of measuring. The core teaching move is to make the strategic saving visible — run the clever route alongside the grind — and to build fluent movement between fraction/decimal/percentage forms so the child reaches for the handiest one and can say why.
misconceptions: Runs the standard column algorithm for 25×16 without looking for factor pairs that make it a mental step
Converts laboriously every time instead of recognising 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as the same number
Measures a missing angle with a protractor rather than deducing it from an angle fact
Picks the fraction/decimal/percentage form by habit rather than by which is efficient for the task

activities.title: Factor-pair regrouping run beside the column method
steps: Work out 25×16 without the column algorithm, splitting 16 into 4×4, then pairing one 4 with 25 to make 100, so the product collapses to 100×4 = 400 in two moves
Carry out the column method for 25×16 as well, and compare how many steps each route took
State the 'hinge' that made the shortcut work (25×4 = 100) and explain why spotting it saved effort
Try the same thinking on 50×16 and 25×24: regroup each to a friendly round number (50×2×8 = 100×8 = 800; 25×4×6 = 100×6 = 600) and show the route
Test a non-example, 23×16: try to find a neat factor pair to a hundred and explain why 25×16 is 'luckier'
activities.insight: A hard-looking multiplication can dissolve when you spot a factor pair that builds a friendly round number (here 25×4 = 100); recognising WHAT makes a shortcut available is the skill, not just reaching the answer.

activities.title: One quantity in three forms: choose the handiest
steps: Look at a single amount shown at once as 3/4, 0.75 and 75% (on a bar or number line marking the same point) and confirm they are one number
Find 75% of £80 and decide whether to use 75%, 0.75 or 3/4; show that 3/4 gives ÷4 then ×3 = £60 in one line
For 30% of £90, decide between 0.3, 3/10 or 30% and justify the choice (3/10 of £90 = £27)
Then try 12.5% of £80 and notice whether the handiest form changes (e.g. 1/8 of 80 = £10), explaining why the best form depends on the numbers
activities.insight: A fraction, decimal and percentage can name the same quantity, so a flexible solver selects whichever form makes the particular numbers easiest instead of converting by habit.

activities.title: Deduce missing angles instead of measuring
steps: Given a diagram where measuring is awkward or impossible, find the missing angle by using a fact (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, around a point 360°, or vertically opposite angles equal)
Name which fact you leaned on and show the working (e.g. 180° − known angle, or 'these two are vertically opposite so they are equal')
Explain how you know the answer is right without a protractor

Extend to a regular polygon: use its equal angles/sides with a known fact (e.g. one given angle, or the equal angles at the centre adding up to 360°) to find unknown angles systematically rather than measuring each one
activities.insight: Angle facts are deductive tools: depending on the fact you either subtract the given parts from a known total (180° on a line, 360° around a point) or set vertically opposite angles equal — both give an exact answer, unlike the approximation of measuring.

activities.title: Explain the choice: a tap-to-reveal and short explanation
steps: Match or reveal FDP equivalents (0.75 = 3/4 = 75%) and annotate a worked angle diagram to consolidate the facts
After solving, answer 'which route/form did you choose and why was it quickest?' in your own words
Compare your chosen route against a slower alternative and state what made the difference
activities.insight: Being able to state WHY a route is efficient — not just getting the answer — is the sign of structural thinking; the answer alone can be reached by grinding.

checkQuestion: Work out 25 × 16 in the cleverest way you can — no column method — and tell me how you spotted the shortcut. Then: to find 75% of £80, would you rather work with 75%, 0.75 or 3/4, and why?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for exploiting factor pairs (25×16 = 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400 because 25×4 makes 100) and for choosing 3/4 of £80 as easiest (÷4 then ×3 = £60) with a reason about which form suits the number. The reasoning about WHY the route is efficient is the target.
